claims.text: A gradient nanostructured heterostructure can overcome the traditional strength-ductility trade-off.
Combining refined-grain regions with coarser microstructural zones enables the strength-ductility trade-off to be overcome.
A conventionally processed homogeneous microstructure with uniform grain size exhibits a trade-off between high strength and limited ductility.
Controlled severe plastic deformation followed by thermal treatment can create a heterogeneous microstructure with a grain-size gradient.
Tight control of temperature and deformation is needed to form a spatially graded structure without phase instability or excessive defects.
Gradients in grain size and crystallographic texture produce distinct hard and soft regions.
A heterogeneous microstructure redistributes local strain.
Nanograined regions increase strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarser-grained regions provide ductility by permitting more uniform plastic deformation.
The strain gradient between hard and soft regions promotes additional work hardening.
Additional work hardening generated by the strain gradient delays necking.
A gradient heterogeneous structure will increase yield strength relative to a homogeneous structure.
A gradient heterogeneous structure will improve ductility relative to a homogeneous structure.
Coexisting microstructural zones provide complementary mechanical performance.
The proposed approach applies to materials that tolerate aggressive grain refinement without detrimental phase transformations.
Certain copper, aluminum, and steel systems may tolerate the proposed gradient-grain processing approach.
The approach may not apply when processing-induced heterogeneity causes embrittlement.
The magnitude of strength and ductility improvements depends on processing parameters and material system.
